about: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) and for Agentic Applications (2026) assessed against what the gateway and the estate around it demonstrably do. Deployer-side view: SecuRAX runs and governs models, it does not train them. Each title is OWASP's category name; the notes are our own assessment and can be wrong: challenge them.

source.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) and Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026)
source.issued: OWASP GenAI Security Project, November 2024 and December 2025
source.caveat: Category names from OWASP's lists (the agentic names as reported by secondary sources; confirm against the official page). Status is our own judgement.

items.title: Prompt injection
items.note: Input rails for injection, jailbreak and hidden-character smuggling on every text part, tool results and the system context; the red team scores it in the purple loop.

items.title: Sensitive information disclosure
items.note: India-aware PII redaction on the way in, secret and personal-data rails on the way out, and residency routing that keeps local data off cloud models.

items.title: Supply chain
items.note: Model weights must match an approved digest (ai check), pickle-format weights are scanned for code, third-party skills pass the vet gate, and every image is pinned and licence-listed.

items.title: Data and model poisoning
items.note: Poisoned weights are caught by the digest check; documents added to a knowledge base are not yet scanned or owner-tagged at retrieval.
items.next: Per-document owner and class at retrieval, and a scan of documents on ingestion (doc 105, G15).

items.title: Improper output handling
items.note: Output rails withhold exfiltration links, active HTML and leaked secrets before an answer reaches the caller.

items.title: Excessive agency
items.note: Tool calls pass an allow, deny and approval policy that fails closed, dangerous arguments are blocked, and one command stops all AI; a call needing approval is refused rather than queued for a person.
items.next: An approval queue: the call waits for a person's yes from the Command Center or the phone (doc 105, G3).

items.title: System prompt leakage
items.note: Canary tokens in system prompts are caught on the way out, and the red team probes for leakage.

items.title: Vector and embedding weaknesses
items.note: Retrieved text arriving as system context is inspected like any prompt: hidden-character smuggling and exfiltration requests are blocked, a plain override is recorded but not blocked (the purple loop shows it, G15); the vector store itself has no per-document access control.
items.next: Per-document owner and class checked at retrieval (doc 105, G15).

items.title: Misinformation
items.note: An honesty check that catches guessing, a careful check-and-rewrite pass, and stale-fact warnings; no answer-quality set runs on each model change.
items.next: An answer-quality set run on every model change, scored over time (doc 105, G6).

items.title: Unbounded consumption
items.note: Per-caller daily and monthly token allowances, request slots and timeouts; a caller over the allowance is refused.

items.title: Agent goal hijack
items.note: Tool results and retrieved context pass the same injection rails as user text, so an instruction hidden in content is caught; there is no separate check that a plan still serves the user's goal.
items.next: Red-team probes for goal hijack through tool output in the purple loop (doc 105, G5).

items.title: Tool misuse and exploitation
items.note: Allow and deny lists with glob patterns, dangerous-argument rules, secrets in arguments blocked and personal data redacted.
items.next: The approval queue for calls that need a person (doc 105, G3).

items.title: Identity and privilege abuse
items.note: Every caller is identified (signed tokens or hashed service keys, roles, an MFA claim, lock-out), and the audit log records who did what.

items.title: Agentic supply chain
items.note: Third-party skills and plugins are vetted before use, the MCP bridge is read-only, and model weights are digest-checked.

items.title: Unexpected code execution
items.note: Untrusted files are inspected in a sandbox, and weight files are scanned for code that would run on load; agents themselves run no generated code.
items.next: Red-team probes that try to make an agent run code (doc 105, G5).

items.title: Memory and context poisoning
items.note: The whole conversation is inspected, earlier assistant turns included: an override planted in chat history or a replayed memory is caught like any untrusted input, not trusted for wearing the model's role. The purple loop fires it as an attack (history-poisoning) and proves it is blocked. The gateway keeps no server-side memory store of its own.
items.next: If a persistent chat-memory store is added, it inherits this inspection and gains a per-account off switch and review (doc 105, G10).

items.title: Insecure inter-agent communication
items.note: Every service-to-service hop can run over internal TLS with verified names; agents do not yet sign or authenticate messages to each other.
items.next: Per-agent identity on calls between agents, checked by the gateway.

items.title: Cascading failures
items.note: A failing detector fails closed, a provider failure falls back down the ladder, and one command stops all AI; there is no automatic breaker that stops a looping agent.
items.next: An automatic breaker that stops an agent whose calls repeat or fail in a loop.

items.title: Human-agent trust exploitation
items.note: Writes an agent proposes wait for a person (the approved-action executor), and the honesty check catches made-up answers.
items.next: Show the person the evidence behind each proposed action before they approve it.

items.title: Rogue agents
items.note: A per-model or all-AI stop with no restart, a per-agent allowance, and a hash-chained audit log that shows what each agent did.
